1.note: Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the members of the tribe of Benjamin were **sons of Benjamin**. He means the people who are descended from Benjamin. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [descendants of Benjamin]
The word **Tekoa** is the name of a town located south of Jerusalem.
The word **Beth Haccherem** is the name of a town near Jerusalem.

Jeremiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

1.q: כִּ֥י רָעָ֛ה נִשְׁקְפָ֥ה מִ⁠צָּפ֖וֹן וְ⁠שֶׁ֥בֶר גָּדֽוֹל
1.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For evil looks down from the north, and with evil comes a great collapse]

Jeremiah is speaking of **evil** as if it were a living thing that could look down on Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For evil is about to come upon you from the north]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the ruin that is coming on the nation were **a great collapse**, that is, a structure breaking into pieces. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and great destruction]

2.note: Here Jeremiah is speaking of the city of Jerusalem and the people who live there as if they were a young woman, **the daughter of Zion**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the city of Jerusalem]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the beautiful and delicate woman** is lovely and unused to hardship, so is **the daughter of Zion**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I compare the daughter of Zion to a woman who is lovely and unaccustomed to hardship]

3.note: Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the enemy kings and the armies who will come against Jerusalem were **shepherds and their flocks**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [To them kings and their armies will go like shepherds with their flocks]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the enemy commanders plundering the part of the city assigned to each of them were shepherds letting their flocks **pasture** in an assigned area. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they shall plunder each one the part assigned to him]

4.note: Jeremiah does not use an introductory phrase to indicate that the words that begin here are the words of the army that is attacking Jerusalem. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [The commanders told their troops,]

The attackers are using **Consecrate {yourselves for} war** as a common expression of the culture to mean “perform the religious ceremonies that prepare an army to fight.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Prepare for battle against her with the proper religious rites]

The attackers are using **Woe to us** as a common expression of the culture to mean “it is terrible for us.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Bad news for us]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [for it is late in the day and the light will soon be gone]

The attackers are using **the day faces away** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the daylight is fading.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the daylight is almost gone]

6.note: The expression **For thus says Yahweh of Armies** introduces a direct quotation that continues to the end of the following verses. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [For this is what Yahweh, commander of the heavenly armies, says]

6.q: כִּרְת֣וּ עֵצָ֔ה וְ⁠שִׁפְכ֥וּ עַל יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם סֹלְלָ֑ה
6.note: The implication is that Yahweh is giving these commands to the army that will attack Jerusalem, not to the people of the city. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You enemy soldiers, cut a tree, and heap up siegeworks against Jerusalem]

The implication is that Jerusalem deserves what Yahweh is bringing on her. This could mean: (1) she is the city that must be punished or (2) she is the city that has been abandoned. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [is the city marked out for punishment]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **oppression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [she is full of oppression]

Here, **all of her** represents all of the people who live in the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of her people practice oppression in her midst]

7.q: כְּ⁠הָקִ֥יר בור מֵימֶ֔י⁠הָ כֵּ֖ן הֵקֵ֣רָה רָעָתָ֑⁠הּ
7.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a well** constantly supplies fresh water, so the city constantly produces more **evil**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [She never stops producing new evil]

The expression **are heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People hear violence and oppression in her]

Here, **Violence and oppression** represents the impact, presented as noise, that violent and oppressive deeds make. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The noise of violent and oppressive deeds is heard in her]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Violence** and **oppression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [People acting violently and cruelly harm others in her]
Here, **before my face** represents being in Yahweh’s sight. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my sight]

8.q: הִוָּסְרִי֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם פֶּן תֵּקַ֥ע נַפְשִׁ֖⁠י מִמֵּ֑⁠ךְ פֶּן אֲשִׂימֵ֣⁠ךְ שְׁמָמָ֔ה אֶ֖רֶץ ל֥וֹא נוֹשָֽׁבָה
8.note: Here, **lest** marks **my soul turns away in disgust from you** and **I make you a wasteland** as the outcomes that the warning **Let yourself be instructed, Jerusalem** is meant to prevent. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

The expression **be instructed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let me instruct you, Jerusalem]

Here, **Jerusalem** represents the people who live in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let yourselves be instructed, you inhabitants of Jerusalem]

Here, **my soul** represents Yahweh himself, the one who is speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [lest I turn away in disgust from you]

The expression **not inhabited** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a land that no people inhabit]

The phrase **a wasteland, a land not inhabited** expresses a single idea. The phrase **not inhabited** tells more about **a wasteland**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a wasteland where no one lives]

9.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the remnant of Israel** before the information about what will happen to them. Alternate translation: [As for the remnant of Israel, they will surely glean them like a vine]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the vine** is stripped completely bare by those who harvest it, so is **the remnant of Israel** stripped bare by their enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They will completely plunder the remnant of Israel, just as harvesters pick a vine clean of every last grape]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **glean** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [They will thoroughly glean]

The word **your** is singular here, even though the verbs earlier in the verse are plural. Yahweh is addressing the enemy that he is sending against Israel as if it were a single person. Use a singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using **Cause your hand to return** as a common expression of the culture to mean “go back over the vines a second time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Go back over the vines again]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a grape gatherer** goes back **over the branches** to pick every grape he can find, so the enemy will come back to seize whatever the people of Israel have left. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as a grape gatherer does when he searches the branches again to take every last grape]

10.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to express his despair that no one is willing to listen to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one to whom I can speak and give warning who will listen!]

The pronoun **I** refers to Jeremiah, not to Yahweh, who was the speaker in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [To whom shall I, Jeremiah, speak and give warning]
See how you translated “listen” in 3:13. Alternate translation: [that they may obey]

Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the refusal of the people to listen were an ear that was **uncircumcised**, that is, a body part that had not been set apart for Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They are unwilling to listen]

Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

The implication is that the people do not welcome what Yahweh says to them. This could mean: (1) that they treat the word of Yahweh as something shameful or (2) that the word of Yahweh brings shame on them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They regard the word of Yahweh as something shameful]

11.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why Yahweh’s anger fills me also]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the anger of Yahweh, **the heat of Yahweh**, were a hot liquid that had filled him up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Therefore, I feel the same intense anger that Yahweh feels]

Jeremiah is using this possessive form to mean the anger that Yahweh feels toward his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the anger that Yahweh feels]

Jeremiah does not use an introductory phrase to indicate that the words that begin here are the words of Yahweh rather than his own. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his anger were a liquid that Jeremiah could **Pour** out on people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Unleash it on the children outside]

The expression **will be captured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the enemy will capture a husband together with a wife]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [an old person will be captured with one full of days]

Yahweh is using **fullness of days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “very advanced in age.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [an old person who is very advanced in age]

12.note: The expression **will be turned over** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And I will turn their houses over to others]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and their fields and their wives will be given away as well]

12.q: כִּֽי אַטֶּ֧ה אֶת יָדִ֛⁠י עַל יֹשְׁבֵ֥י הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ
12.note: Yahweh is using **stretch out my hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “act with power in order to punish.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For I shall act powerfully to punish the inhabitants of the land]

13.note: Yahweh is referring to all of the people by naming two extremes, **the smallest** and **the greatest**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [For without exception]

Here, the terms **prophet** and **priest** represent all the religious leaders of the people, without exception. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And all the leaders of the people, without exception]

14.q: וַֽ⁠יְרַפְּא֞וּ אֶת שֶׁ֤בֶר עַמִּ⁠י֙ עַל נְקַלָּ֔ה
14.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the ruin that has come on his people were a **wound** that the prophets and priests could heal. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they have treated the ruin of my people as if it were something minor]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [declaring repeatedly that all is well, but there is no]

The prophets and priests are repeating the word **Peace** in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [All is very well]

15.note: Yahweh is using the question form to assert that the people felt no shame at all. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [They felt no shame at all when they did an abomination!]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **an abomination**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when they did what is detestable] or [when they did what is abominable]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **ashamed** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [they were not ashamed at all]

Yahweh is using **blush** as a common expression of the culture to mean “show shame.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they did not even know how to show shame]

Here, **fall** represents die in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Therefore, they will die in battle among those who have been killed]

The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result]

16.q: עִמְדוּ֩ עַל דְּרָכִ֨ים וּ⁠רְא֜וּ וְ⁠שַׁאֲל֣וּ לִ⁠נְתִב֣וֹת עוֹלָ֗ם אֵי זֶ֨ה דֶ֤רֶךְ הַ⁠טּוֹב֙ וּ⁠לְכוּ בָ֔⁠הּ
16.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the way people live were roads and **paths** on which they could **walk**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Consider carefully the ways people live and ask about the customs of long ago, which manner of life is good; and live that way]
Here, **your souls** represents themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and find rest for yourselves]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Judah, the same people whom Yahweh has just been addressing directly. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But the people of Judah said]

17.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the prophets he sent to warn his people were **watchmen** posted on the wall of a city. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I appointed prophets to warn you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the warnings his prophets gave were **the sound of the horn** that a watchman blows to alert a city. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention to the warnings they give]

18.note: Yahweh is speaking to the **nations**, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people of Judah who are listening to him that he feels very strongly about their refusal to obey him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the nations. Alternate translation: [Therefore, I am summoning the nations to hear this]

The implication is that Yahweh is summoning witnesses to observe what he is about to do. This could mean: (1) what Yahweh will do to the people of Judah or (2) what will happen among them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And know, you assembled witnesses, what I am about to do to them]

19.note: Here, **earth** represents the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Hear, O people who live on the earth]

Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the outcome that their plans produce. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the result that their plans have produced]

19.q: אָנֹכִ֜י מֵבִ֥יא רָעָ֛ה אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה פְּרִ֣י מַחְשְׁבוֹתָ֑⁠ם
19.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I shall bring disaster to this people, the disaster that is the fruit of their plans]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the consequences of what the people planned were **fruit** that grew from those plans. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the consequences of what they planned]

19.q: כִּ֤י עַל דְּבָרַ⁠י֙ לֹ֣א הִקְשִׁ֔יבוּ וְ⁠תוֹרָתִ֖⁠י וַ⁠יִּמְאֲסוּ בָֽ⁠הּ
19.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what the people did before the information about **my words** and **my law**. Alternate translation: [For they did not pay attention to my words, and they rejected my law]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For to my words they did not pay attention, and to my law they did not pay attention either]

20.q: לָ⁠מָּה זֶּ֨ה לִ֤⁠י לְבוֹנָה֙ מִ⁠שְּׁבָ֣א תָב֔וֹא וְ⁠קָנֶ֥ה הַ⁠טּ֖וֹב מֵ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מֶרְחָ֑ק
20.note: Yahweh is using the question form to reject the offerings of the people as worthless to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Frankincense coming from Sheba means nothing to me! And neither does reed perfume from a distant land!]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Or what is this to me, reed perfume coming from a distant land]

A **reed perfume** is a kind of sweet-smelling substance made from an aromatic cane that grew in far-off lands. If your readers would not be familiar with what a reed perfume is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [Or sweet-smelling spice]

20.q: עֹלֽוֹתֵי⁠כֶם֙ לֹ֣א לְ⁠רָצ֔וֹן וְ⁠זִבְחֵי⁠כֶ֖ם לֹא עָ֥רְבוּ לִֽ⁠י
20.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I do not accept any of your offerings at all]

21.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why]

Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look, I]

21.q: הִנְ⁠נִ֥י נֹתֵ֛ן אֶל הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה מִכְשֹׁלִ֑ים וְ⁠כָ֣שְׁלוּ בָ֠⁠ם
21.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the ruin he is bringing on his people were **stumbling blocks** that he was setting in their path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, I shall bring ruin on this people, and they will be destroyed by it]

Here the masculine terms **fathers** and **sons** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [parents and children together]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **resident** or a specific **neighbor**. He means residents and neighbors in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Residents and their neighbors will perish]

22.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention, a people is coming from the land of the north]

The implication is that Yahweh is describing the Babylonians, who would invade Judah from the north. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the land of the north, that is, from Babylon]

The expression **is being woken up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I am rousing a great nation]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the nation that is preparing to attack were a sleeper who was **being woken up**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a great nation is being stirred to action]

Yahweh says **from the farthest parts of the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [from a land very far away]

23.note: The terms **cruel** and **not compassionate** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They are utterly merciless]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the sea** is loud and overpowering, so is the noise that this army makes as it advances. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Their noise is loud and overwhelming]

The expression **arranged** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [taking their positions like men for battle]

The point of this comparison is that just as **men for battle** are drawn up in ordered ranks, so are these soldiers as they advance against Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [drawn up in ordered ranks as an army ready to fight]

24.note: Jeremiah does not use an introductory phrase to indicate that the words that begin here are the words of the people of Jerusalem rather than the words of Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [The people responded,]

Here the people of Jerusalem are speaking as if their loss of strength and courage were their **hands** going limp. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we lose all our strength]

The people of Jerusalem are speaking of **Distress** as if it were a living thing that could take hold of them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We have become distressed]

The people of Jerusalem are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Distress seizes us as anguish seizes a woman giving birth]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a woman giving birth** is overcome by sudden and intense pain, so are the people of Jerusalem overcome by fear of the enemy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [anguish as intense and sudden as the pain of a woman giving birth]

25.q: אַל תצאי הַ⁠שָּׂדֶ֔ה וּ⁠בַ⁠דֶּ֖רֶךְ אַל תלכי
25.note: The commands **Do not go out** and **do not walk** are singular in form, because Jeremiah is addressing the city as if it were one single woman. Since he means all of the people who live there, use whatever form would be natural in your language for addressing a whole group.

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [for the sword of the enemy is there, and there is terror from all around]

Here, **the sword** represents armed attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the violent attack of the enemy]

Here, **terror** represents the enemy who causes terror. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [terrifying attackers from all around]

26.note: Here Jeremiah is speaking of his fellow Israelites as if they were a single young woman, **Daughter of my people**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My beloved people]

Putting on sackcloth and rolling **about in ash** was a symbolic action by which people in this culture showed that they were in deep grief. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [gird yourself with sackcloth and roll about in ash to show your deep grief]

The point of this comparison is that just as the death of **an only son** brings a family the deepest grief they can know, so is the grief that these people should show over the disaster that is coming. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [make mourning for yourself with the deepest grief that a family feels when their only son dies]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe a **lamentation** that is characterized by **bitterness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a bitter lamentation]

27.note: Jeremiah does not use an introductory phrase to indicate that Yahweh is now speaking to him. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. See the UST.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Jeremiah were **a tester** and **an appraiser**, that is, a metalworker who tests metal to find out whether it is pure. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have appointed you to examine my people, to evaluate them carefully]

28.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **gossip**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [going about spreading harmful rumors]

Yahweh is using **going about {in} gossip** as a common expression of the culture to mean “habitually spreading damaging reports about other people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [habitually spreading damaging reports about other people]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people were **bronze and iron**, hard and common metals, rather than precious silver which is malleable. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All of them are hard and worthless]

29.note: **The bellows** is a device that a metalworker pumps in order to force air into a fire to make it burn hotter. If your readers would not be familiar with what bellows are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [The air pumps]

29.q: לַ⁠שָּׁוְא֙ צָרַ֣ף צָר֔וֹף וְ⁠רָעִ֖ים לֹ֥א נִתָּֽקוּ
29.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if his effort to make his people pure were the failed attempt of a metalworker to **refine** silver. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In vain he tries repeatedly to make his people pure, but the wicked ones are not removed from among them]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **refines** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [he keeps on refining]

The expression **are not torn away** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but the evil things do not tear away]

30.note: The expression **will be called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People will call them, ‘rejected silver,’]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his people were **rejected silver**, metal that a refiner has thrown away because it could not be made pure. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people who are worthless and cast aside]
